report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not supported by credible evidence. Studies testing both specific vaccines and the *cumulative immune/antigen exposure* from multiple childhood vaccines have not found that greater vaccination causes autism.

**Most directly relevant evidence:** A 2013 U.S. case-control study used immunization registries and medical records to total the antibody-stimulating proteins and polysaccharides received by children. It found no association between greater antigen exposure in the first two years of life and autism, including autism with regression. This addresses the “too many, too soon” version of the claim more directly than studies of a single vaccine.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/

A 2014 meta-analysis concluded that vaccination was not associated with autism or autism-spectrum disorder; it also found no association for thimerosal/mercury or MMR. Meta-analyses pool results across studies and are useful because any genuine sizeable effect should emerge consistently.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X14006367

The original MMR concern has likewise been tested in population-level cohorts. A Danish study following children born 1991–1998 found no increased autism risk among MMR-vaccinated children.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa021134

More recently, a nationwide Danish cohort of over 1.2 million children examined differing cumulative exposure to aluminum-adsorbed childhood vaccines and found no association with neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40658954/

The idea can seem persuasive because autism signs are often recognized during the same early-childhood period when many vaccines are given. Timing alone, however, cannot establish causation; the controlled studies above compare vaccinated exposure levels and outcomes directly.
